implementation_notes: Go already returns errors instead of throwing, so the pattern reduces to 'do not return early': append every failure to a []error slice, keep checking, and return errors.Join(errs...), which is nil when all checks passed and otherwise wraps every entry so errors.Is/As can see each of them. errors.Join is stdlib since Go 1.20; before that the same loop needed a custom multi-error type. When entries must carry field names and codes rather than an error tree, model a struct with an Errors field or use the validator variant.
pitfalls: The Go habit if err != nil { return err } is fail-fast; inside an accumulating validator every early return silently drops the remaining errors.
errors.Join does not flatten the result into a list: callers must use errors.Is/errors.As or the Unwrap() []error form, and its message is newline-joined prose.
Joining the same sentinel twice (or a nil slice) is easy to get wrong - errors.Join drops nils, but duplicate sentences still reach the user.

variants.name: go-playground/validator struct tags
variants.implementation_notes: The declarative alternative in Go: describe each field's constraints in a struct tag and call validate.Struct(req); on failure the returned error is a validator.ValidationErrors slice holding one FieldError per failed tag, which you map to the API's field/code pairs. Choose it when the constraints are numerous and uniform; keep the errors.Join form when the checks need application state or cross-field context.
pitfalls: A failure inside a nested struct arrives with a Namespace path; reporting fe.Field() alone loses where in the payload the problem sits.
An error that is not validator.ValidationErrors (an InvalidValidationError) means the call itself was wrong - type-assert before iterating.
Tags are strings: a typo is only discovered when validation first runs, so cover the tags with a test.
